question: Under Md. Code Ann., Business Occupations and Professions §17-501, "trust money" is best defined as:
choice_a: Commission income the broker has already earned and collected at closing
choice_b: The broker's own operating funds used to pay office overhead and staff salaries
choice_c: A deposit, payment, or other money a person entrusts to a real estate broker to hold for the benefit of the owner or another beneficial owner in connection with a real estate transaction
choice_d: Money paid directly by a buyer to a title company at settlement, bypassing the broker entirely
explanation: Section 17-501 defines trust money as money a person entrusts to a real estate broker to hold for the benefit of the owner or a beneficial owner in connection with a Maryland real estate transaction. It is not the broker's own money and is held for someone else's benefit.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-501 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-502, within how many business days after acceptance of a contract of sale by both parties must a Maryland broker deposit trust money into a proper trust account?
choice_a: 24 hours
choice_b: 3 business days
choice_c: 10 business days
choice_d: 7 business days
explanation: Section 17-502(b)(1) requires a broker to deposit trust money within 7 business days after acceptance of a contract of sale by both parties, into an account maintained separately from the broker's own funds and used solely for trust money.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-502(b)(1) (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-502(a), when an associate broker or salesperson receives trust money in the course of providing real estate services, that licensee must:
choice_a: Promptly submit the trust money to the supervising broker
choice_b: Deposit the funds directly into the broker's escrow account without informing the broker
choice_c: Hold the funds personally in a labeled envelope until closing
choice_d: Forward the funds directly to the title company handling settlement
explanation: Section 17-502(a) requires associate brokers and salespersons to promptly submit trust money they receive to their supervising broker, who then bears the statutory deposit obligations under the subtitle.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-502(a) (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-503, a Maryland real estate broker must deposit trust money into a financial institution that is:
choice_a: Any federally insured institution located anywhere in the United States
choice_b: Located in Maryland and insured by an entity such as the FDIC, NCUA, or a State deposit insurance fund
choice_c: An interest-bearing money market mutual fund regardless of location
choice_d: A licensed title company's own escrow department
explanation: Section 17-503 requires trust money to be deposited in a financial institution located in the State whose deposits are insured by the FDIC, FSLIC, NCUA, the State of Maryland Deposit Insurance Fund Corporation, or the Credit Union Insurance Corporation.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-503 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Absent written instructions to the contrary from the owner and beneficial owner, §17-504 permits a broker to deposit trust money only in:
choice_a: An interest-bearing account with the interest retained by the broker as compensation
choice_b: A certificate of deposit chosen at the broker's sole discretion
choice_c: A noninterest-bearing checking account, a noninterest-bearing savings account, or a combination of these
choice_d: An attorney's IOLTA trust account instead of the broker's own trust account
explanation: Section 17-504 limits brokers, absent contrary written instructions, to noninterest-bearing checking or savings accounts (or a combination) for holding trust money.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-504 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-505, before distributing unclaimed trust funds a broker must give the parties written notice of intended distribution, after which either party may protest in writing within how many days?
choice_a: 10 days
choice_b: 15 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: 30 days
explanation: Section 17-505 requires the broker to notify both parties in writing of an intended distribution of trust funds, and gives either party 30 days from delivery of that notice to protest by hand delivery or certified mail.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-505 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-505, a real estate broker holding trust money may invest that money only:
choice_a: As the parties instruct in writing, or under a mutual written agreement among the parties
choice_b: At the broker's sole discretion, so long as the broker believes it benefits the parties
choice_c: In any FDIC-insured certificate of deposit without needing party consent
choice_d: Only after obtaining pre-approval from the Real Estate Commission for each investment
explanation: Section 17-505 restricts a broker's investment of trust money to instances where the parties have given written instructions or reached a mutual written agreement authorizing the investment.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-505 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-507, how long must a Maryland broker retain copies of listings and transaction records after closing of a real estate transaction?
choice_a: 3 years, starting on the date of closing
choice_b: 5 years, starting on the date of closing
choice_c: 7 years, starting on the date of closing
choice_d: 2 years, starting on the date of closing
explanation: Section 17-507 requires brokers to retain copies of listings and transaction documents for 5 years starting on the date of closing of a real estate transaction.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-507 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-507, for a listing that never results in a closed transaction, how long must the broker retain the related records?
choice_a: 1 year after the listing expires
choice_b: 3 years after the listing expires
choice_c: 5 years after the date of the listing
choice_d: No retention is required if the transaction never closes
explanation: Section 17-507 requires that for transactions that do not close, records be retained for 5 years after the date of the listing, the same 5-year baseline used elsewhere in the recordkeeping statute.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-507 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-507, where must a broker's trust money records physically be kept?
choice_a: At the broker's personal residence
choice_b: At the closing/title company's office
choice_c: On file with the Maryland Real Estate Commission
choice_d: In a secured area within the office of the broker
explanation: Section 17-507 requires trust money records to be kept in a secured area within the broker's office, ensuring both confidentiality and availability for Commission inspection.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-507 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-507, for a broker's records to be validly maintained in electronic form, the recordkeeping system must ensure that the records:
choice_a: Cannot be erased or altered, are created in the regular course of business, and are indexed for reliable, chronological retrieval
choice_b: Are stored exclusively in the original proprietary software used to create them, with no backup permitted
choice_c: Are printed out and physically re-filed on paper every quarter regardless of the electronic system used
choice_d: Are password-protected but may otherwise be freely edited by the broker after creation
explanation: Section 17-507's electronic recordkeeping provision requires that electronically stored records cannot be erased or edited, are created during the regular course of business, and include reliable indexing for convenient, chronological access.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-507 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under §17-507, if the Real Estate Commission requests paper copies of a broker's electronically stored records during an inspection, who bears the cost of producing those copies?
choice_a: The Real Estate Commission, from its enforcement budget
choice_b: The licensee, at the licensee's own expense
choice_c: The cost is split equally between the broker and the Commission
choice_d: The client whose transaction the records pertain to
explanation: Section 17-507 makes clear that the Commission may inspect records during business hours upon reasonable notice, and the licensee must provide paper copies of requested records at the licensee's own expense.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-507 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.01.07, once a broker establishes a trust or escrow account and receives trust monies, the broker must report the bank's name and account number to the Real Estate Commission:
choice_a: Only if the Commission requests it during a routine audit
choice_b: Within 30 days of the broker's next license renewal
choice_c: As soon as trust monies are received
choice_d: Only if the account is interest-bearing
explanation: COMAR 09.11.01.07(A) requires a broker to report the escrow or special account's bank name and account number to the Commission as soon as trust monies are received, not on a delayed or renewal-linked schedule.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.01.07 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.01.07, if a broker changes escrow accounts, changes the account number, or moves the account to a different bank, written notice to the Real Estate Commission is required within:
choice_a: 24 hours after the action
choice_b: 30 days after the action
choice_c: 60 days after the action
choice_d: 10 days after the action
explanation: COMAR 09.11.01.07 requires written notification to the Commission within 10 days after establishing a new account, changing an account number, or transferring the trust account to a different bank.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.01.07 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.01.18, if parties to a transaction dispute how held deposit monies should be distributed and no signed releases exist, one lawful option available to the licensee is to:
choice_a: File a bill of interpleader in the proper circuit court, depositing the funds into the court's registry
choice_b: Release the funds to whichever party demands them first, in writing
choice_c: Retain the funds indefinitely with no further action required
choice_d: Return the funds only to the seller regardless of which party is entitled to them
explanation: COMAR 09.11.01.18 gives a licensee holding disputed deposit money several options, including holding the funds until all parties sign releases, filing a bill of interpleader to deposit the funds with the court, holding until a court orders disbursement in a filed suit, or distributing per Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-505.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.01.18 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-320 and COMAR 09.11.05.02, a Maryland real estate broker has a statutory duty to:
choice_a: Personally review and approve every listing photograph before it is published online
choice_b: Exercise reasonable and adequate supervision over the provision of real estate brokerage services by any other individual on the broker's behalf
choice_c: Co-sign every sales contract negotiated by an affiliated salesperson
choice_d: Personally countersign every check written from an associate's personal account
explanation: Section 17-320 and its implementing regulation, COMAR 09.11.05.02, require a broker to exercise reasonable and adequate supervision over the real estate brokerage services provided by associate brokers and salespersons affiliated with the broker, regardless of their employment classification.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §17-320; COMAR 09.11.05.02 (live-verified via mgaleg.maryland.gov and regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.05.02, when a branch office has a designated branch office manager, that manager's supervisory duty over agents registered at that office:
choice_a: Completely replaces the broker's supervisory duty for that branch office
choice_b: Applies only to unlicensed clerical staff at the branch
choice_c: Exists in addition to, and does not replace, the broker's own supervisory obligation
choice_d: Is optional and applies only if the branch has more than 10 licensees
explanation: COMAR 09.11.05.02 makes clear that a branch office manager must supervise the associate brokers and salespersons registered at that office, but this duty exists alongside, not in place of, the broker's own overarching supervisory responsibility.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.05.02 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.05.02, the requirement that a broker exercise reasonable and adequate supervision over associate brokers and salespersons:
choice_a: Automatically converts every affiliated licensee into a W-2 employee of the broker
choice_b: Only applies if the broker has designated the licensees as employees rather than independent contractors
choice_c: Is waived entirely for licensees who work from home offices
choice_d: Does not by itself create an employer-employee relationship or change the licensees' independent contractor status
explanation: COMAR 09.11.05.02(C) clarifies that the supervision requirement does not, by itself, establish an employer-employee relationship or alter an associate broker's or salesperson's independent contractor classification.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.05.02 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.05.03, once it is shown that a broker did not provide reasonable and adequate supervision, the burden of proof:
choice_a: Shifts to the broker to show that the supervision actually provided was reasonable and adequate
choice_b: Remains entirely on the Real Estate Commission to prove the broker's supervision was inadequate
choice_c: Shifts to the affiliated associate broker or salesperson to prove the broker's negligence
choice_d: Cannot be resolved administratively and must be litigated in circuit court
explanation: COMAR 09.11.05.03 provides that once a showing is made that the broker did not provide reasonable and adequate supervision, the burden shifts to the broker to demonstrate that the supervision provided was in fact reasonable and adequate.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.05.03 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.05.03, evidence relevant to whether a broker provided reasonable and adequate supervision includes written office policies and:
choice_a: The broker's personal annual sales volume compared to the office average
choice_b: Training or sales meetings held regularly, at least once every 2 months, with attendance records kept
choice_c: The total number of open houses the office hosted that calendar year
choice_d: The broker's total years licensed in states other than Maryland
explanation: COMAR 09.11.05.03 lists factors relevant to adequate supervision, including written procedures covering deposit handling, fair housing, and contract review, plus documented training or sales meetings held at least once every 2 months with attendance records.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.05.03 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under COMAR 09.11.01.23, a newly designated broker, branch office manager, or team leader in Maryland must complete a broker supervision course of at least how many clock hours, within 90 days of the designation taking effect?
choice_a: 3 clock hours
choice_b: 15 clock hours
choice_c: 1.5 clock hours
choice_d: 30 clock hours
explanation: COMAR 09.11.01.23 requires a newly designated broker, branch office manager, or team leader to complete a 1.5 clock-hour broker supervision course within 90 days, unless the course was already completed within the preceding 4 years.
source_note: COMAR 09.11.01.23 (live-verified via regs.maryland.gov)

question: Under Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-105.1, before a secured party may file a foreclosure action on certain residential mortgages, the law generally requires:
choice_a: A court order specifically authorizing the borrower to pursue a short sale
choice_b: Written notice to the local multiple listing service disclosing the pending default
choice_c: Written consent from every real estate broker involved in the original purchase transaction
choice_d: A loss mitigation analysis considering options such as loan modification, a short sale, or deed in lieu of foreclosure
explanation: Real Property §7-105.1 requires secured parties to conduct a loss mitigation analysis and consider available loss mitigation programs -- including short sales, deeds in lieu of foreclosure, and loan modifications -- as alternatives before pursuing foreclosure.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-105.1 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com, cross-referencing mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under Real Property Title 7, Subtitle 3 (Foreclosure Consultants and Foreclosure-Rescue Transactions), a "foreclosure consultant" is generally a person who, for compensation, offers or agrees to:
choice_a: Help a homeowner whose residence is in default stop or postpone a foreclosure sale, obtain forbearance, or avoid impairment of the homeowner's credit
choice_b: List the homeowner's property for sale as the homeowner's licensed real estate broker
choice_c: Provide free HUD-approved housing counseling with no compensation involved
choice_d: Represent the lender at the foreclosure sale itself
explanation: Real Property §7-301 defines a foreclosure consultant as a person who solicits or contacts a homeowner in default and, generally for compensation, offers services such as stopping or postponing a foreclosure sale, obtaining forbearance, or helping avoid credit impairment.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-301 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com, cross-referencing mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under Real Property §7-306, a foreclosure consulting contract must include a boldface notice disclosing to the homeowner that the consultant:
choice_a: Is not required to disclose the sources of the consultant's compensation
choice_b: Cannot ask the homeowner to sign, or have the homeowner sign, any lien, mortgage, or deed unless specifically described in the agreement
choice_c: May charge unlimited advance fees before performing any services
choice_d: Is exempt from this disclosure requirement if the consultant also holds a Maryland real estate broker license
explanation: Real Property §7-306 requires foreclosure consulting contracts to be in at least 12-point type, disclose all compensation, and include a 14-point boldface notice stating the consultant cannot ask the homeowner to sign any lien, mortgage, or deed except as specifically described in the agreement.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-306 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com, cross-referencing mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under Real Property §7-310, a homeowner whose residence is in default and who signs a contract to sell or transfer the residence to a foreclosure-rescue purchaser has the right to rescind that contract within:
choice_a: 3 days after execution of the contract
choice_b: 10 days after execution of the contract
choice_c: 5 days after execution of the contract
choice_d: 15 days after execution of the contract
explanation: Real Property §7-310 gives a homeowner of a residence in default the right to rescind a sale or transfer contract within 5 days after its execution, and bars recording of any deed affecting title during that 5-day rescission period.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-310 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com, cross-referencing mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under Real Property §7-321, a person who violates the Maryland foreclosure consultant/foreclosure-rescue transaction subtitle is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $10,000 and/or imprisonment for up to:
choice_a: 1 year
choice_b: 5 years
choice_c: 6 months
choice_d: 3 years
explanation: Real Property §7-321 makes a violation of the foreclosure consultant/foreclosure-rescue transaction subtitle a misdemeanor subject to imprisonment not exceeding 3 years, a fine not exceeding $10,000, or both.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Real Property §7-321 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com, cross-referencing mgaleg.maryland.gov)

question: Under Md. Code Ann., Business Regulation §8-301 (Maryland Home Improvement Law), a person who sells or performs home improvement work in Maryland must generally hold a license issued by:
choice_a: The Maryland Home Improvement Commission
choice_b: The Maryland Real Estate Commission
choice_c: The local county building permits office only, with no state-level license
choice_d: The Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation
explanation: Business Regulation §8-301 requires a contractor license to act as a contractor, and a salesperson or contractor license to sell a home improvement, in Maryland -- licensure administered by the Maryland Home Improvement Commission, a body distinct from the Real Estate Commission that supervises brokers.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Business Regulation §8-301 (live-verified via codes.findlaw.com)
